subsystems.name: Key encapsulation mechanism
subsystems.role: lets two parties agree on a shared secret key over a public channel, replacing RSA or elliptic-curve key exchange.
parts: a code-based backup scheme selected for future standardisation

subsystems.name: Digital signature schemes
subsystems.role: proves authenticity and integrity of messages, software and certificates.
parts: a further lattice signature still in preparation

subsystems.name: Hybrid modes
subsystems.role: combines a post-quantum exchange with a classical one so security holds unless both break.
parts: X25519 or ECDH combined with ML-KEM

subsystems.name: Symmetric primitives
subsystems.role: bulk encryption and hashing, which quantum computers weaken only modestly.

subsystems.name: Protocol and PKI integration
subsystems.role: where the algorithms actually get used by the world.
parts: X.509 certificate authorities and root programmes
hardware security modules and secure elements

subsystems.name: Migration tooling
subsystems.role: finding and changing every place cryptography is used.

buildSteps.title: Assume the threat is already present
buildSteps.detail: Traffic recorded today can be stored and decrypted once a quantum computer exists — the 'harvest now, decrypt later' problem — so migration starts before the attacker arrives.

buildSteps.title: Inventory existing cryptography
buildSteps.detail: Scan code, firmware, protocols, certificates and hardware to find every RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve use, and record how long each secret must stay safe.

buildSteps.title: Pick algorithms from the standards
buildSteps.detail: Use the NIST-standardised schemes: ML-KEM for key establishment, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA for signatures, with hash-based signatures preferred where conservative, long-lived security matters.

buildSteps.title: Implement them safely
buildSteps.detail: Lattice and hash-based maths are turned into code that runs in constant time, avoids secret-dependent branching and resists timing and side-channel attacks; some libraries undergo formal verification of these properties.

buildSteps.title: Test against reference vectors
buildSteps.detail: Known-answer tests and cross-implementation checks confirm each scheme produces exactly the specified output before it goes anywhere near production.

buildSteps.title: Deploy in hybrid mode first
buildSteps.detail: Protocol stacks negotiate a classical plus post-quantum key exchange, so a flaw in either one alone does not expose the session — this is how browsers, messengers and VPNs have rolled it out.

buildSteps.title: Migrate signatures and certificates
buildSteps.detail: The harder half: replacing long-lived code-signing, firmware-signing and TLS certificates, which requires certificate authorities, trust stores and hardware modules to support larger keys and signatures.

buildSteps.title: Build in crypto-agility
buildSteps.detail: Interfaces and update paths are designed so algorithms can be swapped again, because the parameter sets and schemes may change after further cryptanalysis.

buildSteps.title: Retire the old algorithms
buildSteps.detail: Legacy RSA and elliptic-curve modes are switched off once dependents have moved, on a schedule set by how long data must remain confidential.

prerequisites.tech: Hardness of lattice and coding problems
prerequisites.why: these problems resist all known classical and quantum attacks, but that is an assumption, not a proof — which is why hybrids and hash-based options exist.
public standards published in 2024 define exact key and ciphertext sizes, so independent implementations interoperate.
a mathematically sound scheme can still leak keys through timing or power use; hardened and formally verified code is still maturing.

prerequisites.tech: Protocols that can carry larger keys
prerequisites.why: post-quantum public keys and signatures are kilobytes rather than bytes, so handshakes must be adapted and sometimes fragmented across records.
keys burned into smartcards, industrial devices and old appliances cannot be updated easily or at all.
no cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists yet, so budgets and deadlines depend on informed estimates rather than demonstrated machines.

pathway.milestone: hybrid post-quantum key exchange running by default in major browsers and messaging apps
pathway.unlocks: protection for session traffic against future decryption of recorded data.

pathway.milestone: post-quantum signatures and certificates issued at scale by certificate authorities and trust stores
pathway.unlocks: authenticated connections that no longer depend on RSA or elliptic curves end to end.

pathway.milestone: migration of long-lived secrets: code signing, firmware, VPNs and hardware security modules
pathway.unlocks: protecting software supply chains and devices that must stay trusted for a decade or more.

pathway.milestone: crypto-agility treated as a standing design requirement, with national-security guidance targeting a full transition by the early 2030s
pathway.unlocks: the ability to change algorithms again quickly if a chosen scheme is broken.
